[?] where used = unclear, and suggested transcription. This was generally caused by microphone placement seating in lab, participant speaking quietly, participants speaking together, background noise, mumbling, using unfamiliar, industry terminology references.

Interviewer 1:	Ok: thanks for coming. I’d like to welcome you all. If you can just start by introducing yourself by saying what department you are in and where you went on placement.

Rebecca:	Ok I’m Rebecca and am doing industrial design and technology, so I’m in the design and technology department and I was on placement with [company] last year working in pet foods and pet food packaging.

Alison:	OK I’m Alison and I’m doing Mechanical Engineering at the Wolfson School and I spent last year at [company] doing heat shrinkage stuff.

Sophie:	I’m also doing mechanical engineering and I spent my placement year at [company] working on photocopiers. I had to do some initial design work for the start of a new project and some end design work for a product launch.

Anna:	Hi I’m Anna and I’m doing quantity surveying in the Civil and Building engineering. I was working with the [company] group of construction and I was involved in the financial and building [???] in London.

Interviewer 1:	Ok, were you based on site?

Anna:	Yes I was on site.

Hayley:	I’m Hayley and I’m doing Mechanical engineering [??]. I worked for [company] resource systems last year doing future concepts and SEKA [????] mechanisms.

Carolyn:	Hi, I’m Carolyn and I work for a cargo charter company called [company]. We do air transport management. I spent most of last year travelling around Europe with a company based in [country].

Interviewer 1:	OK, I’ve got a bit of a task for you all now.

Someone enters

Frances:	Hi, is this the engineering focus group?

Interviewer 2:	yes.

Interviewer 1:	When you’re ready do you want to introduce yourself to everybody and let everyone know what you were doing and where you were on placement.

Frances:	yes sure, my Name’s Frances and I’m doing air-transport management. I was in Liverpool working for [company] which is a passenger transport executive for the [region] area.

Interviewer 1:	right I want you to all take a post-it note now and write on a scale of one to five, so write a number down on how committed you feel to a career in engineering or design or air transport based on your experience of placement. One being bad, five being good.

Alison:	so it’s not necessarily going back to the same thing it’s engineering as a whole?

Interviewer 1:	yes. So if you really loved your placement and they really encouraged you to go into engineering it would be five and you definitely don’t want anything to do with your course, or what you were doing on placement, then it would be a one, if that makes sense to everybody. 

[post-it notes filled in]

Interviewer 1:	OK I am going to go around the group and ask you all tell me what you put and explain why you put it. And if anyone’s speaking and they want to chip in and say if they agree or disagree then that’s fine.

Rebecca:	I put a three. Erm it wasn’t that I didn’t enjoy my placement, I had a really good year but I’ve never been that interested in going into design anyway for the last couple of years just because I haven’t really enjoyed doing it that much. Erm, so my placement was really good and I was primarily working in design but they gave me the opportunity to look at loads of different departments as well so it wasn’t an negative on the placement, I actually came out with more because I knew different areas of work that I knew I didn’t want to go into. But I had already made up my mind before I went there that I wasn’t that interested

Alison:	I felt five. Actually it went the other way for me I wasn’t quite sure whilst I was on placement and I had a great year, did loads of stuff that I really enjoyed and got into. There was a lot more that I could get out of engineering.

Sophie:	Ok, I put a five as well. Although I knew that I wanted to do engineering before I went on placement I didn’t fully know what was available to me. During my placement year I was treated as a member of the team. It wasn’t just as a student, I got to work on the projects and see how they worked.

Anna:	I put four because, whilst I enjoyed my placement, some of the things didn’t appeal to me: especially being on site as a woman. Erm the cleanliness and the whole going on site when it’s raining wasn’t good, though I really enjoyed my placement as an engineer.

Hayley:	Five, which is probably a bit misleading because I did want to do engineering and work-placements and stuff before. It reaffirmed after a full year, instead of doing three or four weeks and going ‘that was alright and now I’m going back to Uni and doss about for a bit.’ It was just nice to know that the boredom threshold didn’t actually kill me and I suddenly didn’t go ‘no, this isn’t what I want to do.’

Carolyn:	I put four, I really enjoyed my placement. I want to work within the air industry again. But I don’t think I have much chance working on what I was doing because the company have said that they don’t take women doing what I want to do.

Frances:	I’ve got a three for mine. I really enjoyed my year out and I never considered transport planning I always though I would do something similar but because I got the placement I went for it anyway. I really enjoyed it because it provided me with options and I could go into it after I graduate. And not just in the air industry. But I don’t think I’ll go back into it mainly because I found it, at times, a little bit depressing because things weren’t going the way that I wanted them to and I want to try working in the air industry.

Interviewer 1:	Was anybody surprised at the fact that everyday work could be a little bit boring, or was it exciting all the time?

Alison:	I wouldn’t say that it was always exciting but nothing ever is to be fair is it?

All:	no

Alison:	you are not going to be on the bouncy castle all the time are you? 

Hayley:	I was more impressed by the fact that instead of being customised [unclear], especially in what I was doing, every so often you got something that was really interesting, rather than it going the other way around. If you don’t want to do it you kind of like plod along until it’s like ‘oh I really need to do that.’ And then you are like there and not noticing that you are doing six hours extra overtime this week and all the rest of it, because you just want to be doing it.

Sophie:	I think that is why it makes a difference, like the teams you were in, particularly, you know because I got to work in two different teams. I think, obviously it may have been difficult for them to, sort of have a new student come along, but who you are working with, I found makes, a big difference.

Interviewer 1:	yes, does anyone else think that as well? 

Rebecca:	Yes I had this manager and she was quite controlling over me and I kind of felt she thought she was like my mum, she was always trying to analyse what I was doing and what I was saying and stuff. And when she changed jobs I got a different manager and he gave me a lot more freedom and I enjoyed my placement a lot more like. I felt that I could like run with things a lot more and had more chance to impress instead of being tied-down.

Interviewer 1:	so do you think that you learnt a lot about different managerial styles and things like that?

Hayley:	yes definitely, 

Rebecca:	I mean even with my second manager, which I instantly found more difficult to work with, both of us adapted so that I proved that yes that perhaps I could go and do that on my own. He began to realise that he needed to give me the space to do that. It wasn’t that I had a horrible time with him it was just adapting to that.

Carolyn:	One of the managers I worked with arose out of the fact of whether he trusted or liked you. So the other placement student who was male got a lot more opportunities than, and he wasn’t sure whether or not women could do the jobs given out. So that made it a lot harder.

Interviewer 1:	did you feel that you were having to prove yourself?

Carolyn:	Yes because if I made a mistake then it would be really well picked up and well-made, whereas if the other placement student, who was male, made a small mistake it was brushed aside. He got to do a lot more opportunities than I had.

Interviewer 2:	Anyone else feel like they were treated differently to their, either other students, or did you feel like you were treated differently because you were a student to other members of staff at all?

Rebecca:	with my first manager she’d had students before and she knew a lot about what we had to do and like how student’s fitted into the business but my second manager sort of acquired me because she’d left and he treated me much more like a normal associate. He’d let me go on business trips and have a lot more freedom because he treated me like any other person working for him and he didn’t set any special rules because I was a student.

Interviewer 1:	What were you going to say Anna?

Anna:	well I was going to say that especially for example in the construction industry whereby there are few women, just are both has advantaged/disadvantaged. Sometimes they would look at you like oh you don’t understand this and that, but when you get to do something very well, they basically praise you. Some of my bosses said that you had to work twice as hard as the men because the men are taken for granted: so that motivated you to do more. We are at a disadvantage but also an advantage in a way.

Interviewer 2:	This was your boss that said that to you?

Anna:	yes

Interviewer 2:	were they male or female?

Anna:	Male, well they were like, he just made a comment like as a woman you have to work twice, because you have to prove yourself and work twice as hard they would say ‘what can you offer us as an engineer?’ or something like that. So, I mean they asked do you know anything about construction: why are you doing it? Stuff like that. So the best thing was it motivated me to work harder and that was an advantage in a way. I had to prove myself so it was also a disadvantage sometimes.

Interviewer 1:	how does that make you feel about being in the industry?

Anna:	alright because I am taking it more like a challenge, you know like if it’s a challenge then you are going to prove yourself. If it’s a challenge I am going to prove that I can do something: I can do something better than the other guy on the other hand. So it’s just like a challenge.

Interviewer 2:	do people feel similar to this?

Sophie:	I think in some respects it was [pause] I wouldn’t necessarily use the word advantage but I had managers [unclear] like even the managing director did say that women bring something different to the work place and we actually enjoy that being there. Whether it’s just a different perspective or opinion or the way our minds think of things and they actually really value that where I work so I felt quite lucky to be treated like that.

Alison:	Our guys do that, they actively try to employ at least one female student, just because it will keep the others under control [laughter] because we didn’t get one. When we were interviewed we didn’t get any girls. They were like, ‘no girls? What are we going to do?’ When it’s like half you bring something different to a problem, you look at it in a different way: they see that as a real bonus.

Sophie:	on the other hand I would hate to be employed just because I’m a woman, so you can’t have it both ways 

Alison:	I’m up for that, if I get a job because I’m female fair enough!

Interviewer 1:	does that bother you?

Alison:	no. If I can play it to my advantage then I will. If there’s me and another guy in work, like sort of equal applicants and they go sort of well go well we’ll have her because she’s female: so be it, it’s great.

Sophie:	I’d like to think I got the job because I was capable not because they needed to make numbers up.

Alison:	oh yeah, I wouldn’t like it if there was some guy who was blatantly better than me, but if it’s sort of, I’ve got two CV’s which one do I go for?

Sophie:	I guess we’ll never know.

Rebecca:	I think that on my course we all had to come for an interview before we got here and, like because it’s completely male-dominated my interview was like a complete farce. Like the bloke was just like chatting to me about his holidays and like wanted to show me his holiday pictures and stuff and when I speak to all the blokes on my course they were all like completely grilled. They had to show portfolios. I said to him: ‘do you want to seem my portfolio?’ and he was like ‘well we haven’t actually got time but like we’ll be making you an offer.’ But in the end that’s worked to my disadvantage. At the time I thought it was brilliant, but actually they didn’t look to see if I had the right skills for the course and that’s why I found the course hard. If someone had looked at my work, then they might have gone oh maybe you should have applied for something different. But they didn’t because I was a girl and they said oh well we need more girls. So we won’t bother we’ll just chat about holidays with her [laughter] so yeah

Interviewer 1:	do you wish you had done a different course then?

Rebecca:	erm, I haven’t minded it but I wouldn’t have changed my course while I am here because I don’t mind sticking at it. But I do think that it would have been beneficial to me if they had looked at my worked because it would have been the right time. I was still looking at courses. It would have been more of a two-way thing, so it might have helped me more. It’s not like I begrudge doing the course so it is ok but…

Interviewer 1:	Ok, do you think that your male colleagues on your course, like that went on placement, have similar sort of thoughts to you about how the placement went and what you got out of it? Do you think that there is any difference between male and female experiences of the placement?

Sophie:	as I mentioned before I had two different heads of department. I actually swapped with a guy who was on the same course as me, at Loughborough. So I did his role after six, months and he did mine. And I know for a fact that he didn’t enjoy his experience as much as I did. He feels that it was the type of work he was given and it may have been that I was lucky and fell into projects at the right time but I know that he didn’t have as good as an experience as I did and that’s the only direct comparison I’ve got. I know a lot of other males who did their placement year at the company and really enjoyed it and I equally know a girl that really didn’t.

Carolyn:	I worked with another male student from our course. He really enjoyed it, he’s been offered a job with the company; they want him back at Christmas. Erm, he got bonuses and stuff. I mean he travelled the world, did a lot of stuff I didn’t. I think he really, really enjoyed it and wants to go back and I really enjoyed as well but I think I would have liked to have seen the job in a bit more depth as he did: see the different aspects. He did two different jobs within the year but I just stayed in operations.

Interviewer 1:	do you think that the company treated you both differently?

Carolyn:	yes, and they are fully aware of that, they know that from my colleague who met the managing director. I said that I’m quite interested in a job here and he was like submit you CV and we’ll look over it and he said traditionally we don’t have women in the Cargo department. He said that it was because the boss of that department doesn’t like women. The boss of that department said that it was because the managing director doesn’t like women in that department [laughter] so, we’ll see. He was quite impressed with the work that I did. 

Interviewer 1:	does that attitude not put you off going back to work for them?

Carolyn:	yes. I wouldn’t. I spent a year working really hard and to be told that it is because I’m a woman doesn’t really show me that that’s a company I would want to work for.

Interviewer 2:	Does it put you off engineering in general or just that company?

Carolyn:	I don’t know: the other companies that I have worked for in the industry that I’m in don’t have that problem with who I am. Sometimes they say ‘oh you are living in a male house,’ I have had no problems I mean nothing like this,

Interviewer 1:	was there anything about being in the workplace that surprised anyone? I mean was your placement your first experience of being within the industry?

Sophie:	it was my first experience of being in engineering. I guess I haven’t really thought through what it was I really expected. I knew what I needed to get out of the year in terms of what I wanted to learn in terms of the course etc. But I hadn’t really thought through exactly what I thought the work place would be like or anything so I don’t really have any preconceived ideas.

Interviewer 1:	do you think knowing what the workplace is like will help you when you graduate and start work?

Sophie:	Errm yes I guess so, I guess it will be easier to get into that because you are more relaxed and you know what to expect.

Interviewer 1:	do people agree with that?

Hayley:	yes

[others nod]

Anna:	I have to choose whether to go back in to construction as a contractor of construction or construction as a consultancy. Because within civil building, usually the women end up going for consultancy because it is much more protected. That’s where you stay in the office and you know men are respected as women. When you go on site, the first thing you notice is that they are whistling at you or doing strange things. I mean you share the same toilet and all those funny things. So I am just now trying to make up my mind whether to go into consultancy or to go back onto site.

Interviewer 1:	in the other areas of engineering is there a distinction between the types of roles and the areas that women are more like to go into rather than men?

Sophie:	where I worked it was more in the design and drawing stage and they tended to always have a female in their department and always loads of girls applied. My position, when we came around to interviewing for it this year we barely had any girls that had applied and we didn’t actually interview a single [inaudible].

Alison:	no girls on the shop floor ever. I have never seen a woman on the shop floor. You know welding grinding and whatever: I have seen them in the kind of like manufacturing but I have never seen them on the shop floor. But where I worked it was quite an older workforce down there anyway. So if they are say, fifty, when they would have started you wouldn’t have had a woman so I’m not sure if you are going to start having them now.

Sophie:	we didn’t have any female apprentices for the model shop or anything like that. I know if I took anything in there. I had to be quite prepared to learn how to cut it myself but somebody would always come over and do it for me which is a great advantage because cutting it wearing a smart shirt or whatever when I just want to get on with the next thing I wanted to do. But had I wanted to, I could have probably pressed it and said oh let me do it I want to learn. But that was obviously their territory, their role, their shop and it didn’t really bother me bit some people may have been put off by it.

Interviewer 1:	Carolyn I know you said that women don’t work in the company you were in, but within transport management is there any particular areas that women are likely to go into? 

Carolyn:	I didn’t see that many women and those I did were mainly doing baggage checking or in the offices. Women in the company worked as secretaries or accountants: there are some in passenger but none in cargo.

Hayley:	Mine was fairly good in having female engineers although most of them were systems engineers. But because it is very project based rather than a systems department and you have your analysis department, there is always other women around. I mean one of the group heads had joined as a scholarship, as an apprentice and she was really upset because this was the first year that they had not had any female applicants and things like that. But we had quite a few girls working there and I have never seen a problem with anything.

Interviewer 1:	Frances, did you notice anything in they types of roles?

Frances:	I know that in my job as a placement student I was the first female. They had males in the previous years and they were all from Loughborough. I hear d from somebody: I don’t know whether it was true that they said they wanted a female, so I don’t know if that was another reason why they picked me. But she did say that I was good in the interview. I mean I enjoyed it and there wasn’t any discrimination or anything and they were really, really friendly and I was the only female in the planning section.

Interviewer 2:	does it shock you all that there is not many women in the places that you work or do you kind of expect it.

[all: we expect it]

Rebecca:	you know that from the numbers on your course.

Sophie:	actually from what HAYLEY was saying as well that the [unclear] department had a lot of females so you did interact with them all and you would see them down the floor and that. It wasn’t until the end of my placement that when I interviewed the next people that the joke was made that oh yeah you’ll get another female worker. That’s when it kind of dawned on me that actually they don’t have that many females sitting downstairs and the fact that they won’t see a female of talk to one project work wise for a couple of days [unclear].

Interviewer 1:	do you think it matters that there aren’t more women in engineering?

Rebecca:	no I don’t think it does because if women wanted to do it they would easily be able to. As I said any girl can get onto my course and so if they wanted to they would be there it is just that it just doesn’t attract interest I don’t think.

Sophie:	I think if people aren’t interested in it then there’s point in them doing it. Like you say if they could get onto the course and go through and do the placement or whatever but if they are not interested then..,

Interviewer 2:	does anyone disagree with that?

[long pause]

Sophie:	it would be nice to see more women but there’s a natural progression: there are more now than there were five years ago.

Interviewer 1:	why do you think that more women don’t do engineering?

Sophie:	for a start it’s not glamorous and I guess society has always put engineering as a male role. And realistically it is probably only over the last thirty years that women have really got to work. People before that may have had jobs working, but I think that society is now that even with a couple, even with a child, both people now need to work. Which is probably why we are beginning to see an increase in other roles, but it’s not readily available either. I don’t remember anybody at school talking to me about engineering.

Hayley:	I remember going to like careers interviews about what you would do at university and it was like: ‘I think I’ll do engineering,’ and it was like ‘oh, you are good at maths and science. Why don’t you do like accounting or physics or you can go and be a doctor or if you want to do engineering then you can do physics and then go on and do something else.’ It was like well why can’t I do engineering? He was saying, well it’s an option but you could do all this as well. I was like well I don’t want to do that because that’s really easy and I’ve seen all that I want to do this.

Interviewer 1:	so did you feel like they were discouraging you from being an engineer?

Hayley:	well they weren’t discouraging they just weren’t aware of it. If I went to my physics teachers or people who knew more about it rather than it just being a careers person, handing out leaflets, then they were really encouraging about this. They were like you are great, you have got the grades for it and all the rest of it I hope you do really well, come back and talk to us. It’s just generically if you talking about what subjects you are good at then. If someone’s good at science and maths then you generally think that they are going to do accounting or a science: you are going to do research stuff. You don’t generally go and become and engineer. Engineering is also kind of associated with the ‘go and do an HND at your local college; go and become a fitter somewhere and do an apprenticeship.

Alison:	it’s like oh are you going to fix cars now

[Group nods, yes, yes]

Sophie:	yep like I am a mechanic? I suppose that like mechanical engineering, people don’t know the difference.

Interviewer 1:	Do you think that people don’t know what engineering is?

Sophie:	yes certainly at school yes, I don’t know about anyone else but, I don’t remember anybody coming in and 

Rebecca:	I still really don’t know what it is!

[laughter]

Hayley:	it’s not just that. We know more about what engineering involves than people outside do because I know my dad was an engineer and trained as a fitter. But like my mum it was like ‘I want to be an engineer’, ‘why do you want to go and do something like that?’ Because you do this, it’s like…, in the end she turned around and said why don’t you be an accountant. I was like I don’t want to be an accountant. It’s like you don’t earn money as an engineer you just do this. It was like no you don’t, you can earn this much you can do this. And once when she was presented with all the statistics and all the rest of it she was like yes you want to apply to Imperial and the rest of it and I was like what? You didn’t want me to even do it a minute ago.

Alison:	but that’s not because of being female. I mean blokes get that exactly the same

Hayley:	it’s just that engineering isn’t seen as a profession. It’s like in Germany and other places it’s like you must do a four year degree and it’s a proper profession and you must do this and you must do that. Here it’s like oh you’re an engineer

Alison:	it’s kind of like oh go and play with stuff.

Sophie:	a lot people think that engineers are quite poorly paid considering if you had gone off and done accountancy for instance.., 

Hayley:	there were loads of people this year. I mean they had to do six-tear appretencies at MBDA, they lost three to accounting firms because they just couldn’t make the money back and it’s like they have been give six grand so far to do the apprenticeship but they are more than willing to give it back, because they can go and get so much more by going and doing finance somewhere. Just getting headhunted.

Int: do you think that engineers are undervalued in the UK?

[nods]

Alison:	absolutely

Sophie:	yes

Hayley:	yes

[laughter]

Interviewer 1:	Does everybody agree with that?

All: Yes! [laughter] 

Hayley:	well it’s not so much being undervalued in general as being undervalued by the engineering industry. In places like accountancy it’s like oh we prefer to take engineers at the moment because you are more practical about this and financing people. 

?: Lots of other industries, will come up to you and say, oh you are doing an engineering degree, why don’t you come and work for us? Whereas an engineering company will go oh you can do some design work.

Sophie:	I also put it down to the fact that because it is so male dominated we will obviously lie back and take poor wages or whatever.

Alison:	[inaudible]

Sophie:	it’s kind of true because I would sit and listen to the guys, I worked with a couple of people that had recently finished grad schemes, were aware that other people, some of their friends had gone to other engineering companies, that paid slightly better and some had gone and done totally different careers having done engineering degrees. And they were on a lot more money and so these guys I worked with were well aware of that and would sit there and moan about it but then what were they actually doing about it; they weren’t looking to get more money; they weren’t putting their point forward or anything. We were kind of luck in a way because our managing director, she changed three months into my placement, so there was this new guy came into the company and I think, had they got in at the right time, engineers as a whole, they could have influenced pay etc. But they basically didn’t.

Interviewer 2:	do you think that men tend to jump into engineering more than women do, that it is a more obvious career choice?

Alison:	yes I think it’s more obvious.

Sophie:	I think that some of the older guys that I worked with gossiping with them, I mean they would say my dad did it before me, 

Alison:	and a lot of the guys that did apprenticeships like straight out of school, maybe it was like their only option in a way. It was like right I have got to get a job well, that one, I’ll go and do an engineering apprenticeship! And you know they have got a lot of skill and they absolutely have it and they have built that up but when they went in they didn’t actually know that they were letting themselves in for. Whereas in that age a woman would not have been encouraged to do that, they would have been encouraged to do a different occupation.

Interviewer 1:	why did you want to apply to do engineering? What was it about it that interested you?

Alison:	I thought it looked cool!

[laughter]

Alison:	it’s like my Dad makes submarines: it’s like how cool is that? And I went on work experience and I really enjoyed it and it was like that’s what I want to do.

Interviewer 2:	did you go where your dad works?

Alison:	yeah I went there in like in my year ten work experience I went to an accountants and I hated it. So I was like right I am going to do something different, six month [unclear] work experience, went there, did some shop floor stuff, some design, some manufacturing stuff and yeah, that’s what I want to do.

Sophie:	I did some work experience at year ten at school and at that time I really wanted to join the navy, but didn’t know exactly what that entailed. I managed to get a week’s work experience at the navy which left me with a weekend to fill which I did as a receptionist. I was bored stupid. Even at that age I found that I already knew how to use the computer and write a letter and it wasn’t ever any different. I mean I know I was only there for five days but it was like, day in, day out answer the phone, write letters and from then on I guess I though, right what do I really want to do? I have done a week in the navy, I have done different departments and the most interesting people I met during that week were basically the engineering side. And so basically from that I decided that that was what I wanted to do. It just seemed interesting and, I admit, it’s not constantly interesting but there is something that you can really enjoy.

Interviewer 1:	why did you decide to start?

Anna:	well my dad used to run a construction company and so he used to claim that I did the surveying just to make loads of money [laughter] but he decided that if he was paying for me to do a university degree in construction [?]. Well I wanted to do something in building or architecture, or quantity surveying or something around that area and so I ended up doing quantity surveying: something in property and construction and all that , so that’s how I ended up doing this.

Interviewer 1:	so there’s a couple of people I know who mentioned having family connections in engineering. Has anyone else got connections?

Sophie:	I have never been very far from it: my dad’s self-employed and my mum told me never to marry anyone who is self-employed and my dad told me to go and get a proper job [laughter] so at least I don’t have the hassle of knowing what I am going to earn at beginning of every year [unclear].

Carolyn:	I wanted to join the RAF and I wasn’t really interested in aircraft so I wasn’t a plane spotter. [laughter] and the business side of the course really happened for me.
